MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

probes.note: Vavilov must be found by citation
the cessation example: words, case type refugee_cessation, government won

steps.title: Welcome to iLit
steps.text: A short, guided walk through the real site, using real decisions. You only press Next: I open the pages, type the searches and press the buttons for you. Back goes one step back, Skip section jumps ahead, and Exit or Esc stops. Nothing is saved unless a step says so.

steps.title: The tour follows these tabs
steps.text: Case search to find and read decisions, then Intelligence / Statistics for judges, citations and Federal Court activity, then the Workbench for your files, pinned decisions and document tools. Everything runs without AI, on stored data.
steps.label: Main tabs

steps.title: Find a decision
steps.text: Everything starts with this box: a case name, a citation such as 2019 SCC 65, or a few words from the reasons. First, the filters that narrow any search.
steps.label: Search box

steps.title: Advanced filters
steps.text: Advanced opens the filter panel on the left. Every filter combines with the words in the search box, and the panel counts how many filters are on.
steps.label: Advanced

steps.title: Outcome and court
steps.text: Outcome keeps the decisions the government won, or the ones the individual won. Court limits the search to the Federal Court, the Federal Court of Appeal, the Supreme Court or the RPD. One click each.
steps.label: Outcome and court

steps.title: Case type
steps.text: Case type sorts every decision by the kind of case it is, worked out from the statute provisions it discusses (no AI). Open a group and tick one or more types; I opened Refugee protection.
steps.label: Case type

steps.title: The other filters
steps.text: Decision result (allowed, dismissed and so on), Cases citing a decision you pick, a topic Tag, the Judge, the Minister or government party, and the Decision year. Apply runs the search and Clear resets everything.
steps.label: Decision result

steps.title: An example: cessation, India, Minister won
steps.text: Say you need refugee cessation cases involving India where the Minister won. First a few words that appear in those decisions: citizen of India passport. The words are matched in the decision text.
steps.label: Words from the reasons

steps.title: Add the case type
steps.text: Next the case type: under Refugee protection I ticked Refugee cessation (s. 108).
steps.label: Refugee cessation

steps.title: Add the outcome and search
steps.text: Last, the outcome: Government won, meaning the Minister prevailed. Pressing it runs the search with all three: the words, the case type and the outcome.
steps.label: Government won

steps.title: The matching decisions
steps.text: These are the cessation decisions about India where the Minister won. Each row shows the court, date, judge, outcome, case type and how many decisions cite it.
steps.label: Results

steps.title: Now a general search
steps.text: I cleared the filters and typed Vavilov, the Supreme Court's leading decision on standard of review. Press Next to run the search.
steps.label: Search box

steps.title: A real search
steps.text: I searched for Vavilov. Each result shows the court, date, how the decision came out, and how many decisions cite it. Next opens it.
steps.label: Vavilov

steps.title: The formatted reader
steps.text: This is Vavilov, formatted as a clean document with numbered paragraphs. The header shows the court, date, citation, and how many decisions cite it, it cites, and statutes it refers to.
steps.label: Header

steps.title: Panel and text, side by side
steps.text: The reader has two parts. The left panel gives the recorded outcome, case details and the topics found in the text; the decision text stays readable beside it.
steps.label: Left panel

steps.title: The Outline
steps.text: The Outline lists the decision's sections with their paragraph numbers. I pressed one and the text jumped to it.
steps.label: Outline

steps.title: Citations, statutes and tags in the text
steps.text: Citations (gold), statutes (purple) and topic tags (green) are marked in the text. Each layer switches on or off, to read the decision clean or fully annotated.
steps.label: Layers

steps.title: What a citation points to
steps.text: Rest the pointer on a marked citation and a card shows what it is and the passage it points to. This is the card for one of the authorities Vavilov relies on.

steps.title: Authorities
steps.text: The Authorities tab lists the cases and statutes this decision cites, how often and at which paragraphs.
steps.label: Authorities

steps.title: Jump through the decision by authority
steps.text: Find takes you to each place an authority is cited. I pressed it for the first case in the list, and the text moved to the passage that cites it.
steps.label: Find

steps.title: Intelligence for this decision
steps.text: The Intelligence tab adds the picture around this decision: the judge, how the decision has been cited, and links to the wider citation analysis.
steps.label: Intelligence

steps.title: Keep it on your Workbench
steps.text: Save to Workbench pins a decision to your own list. I saved Vavilov for you; it is waiting on the Workbench later in the tour.
steps.label: Saved
steps.writes: This step pinned Vavilov to the demo Workbench list called Demo analyst. Remove it any time from the Workbench.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.text: Search a judge to see their decisions in the library, how outcomes split, and which authorities they rely on. Name variants are merged so one judge is not split across spellings.

steps.title: One judge's record
steps.text: I opened the first judge in the list. A profile shows that judge's decisions, how they came out, and the authorities they cite.

steps.title: Citation intelligence
steps.text: Start from one authority, here Vavilov, and see who relies on it: which courts and judges cite it, the outcomes of the cases that cite it, the statutes they discuss, and how its use has changed year to year.

steps.title: Federal Court activity
steps.text: FC Analytics covers the classified Federal Court immigration docket: outcomes, timing, motions, judges and counsel, read from the Court's registry entries for each file. Every chart follows the filters: years filed, registry, the decision under review, application type, counsel and language.
steps.label: FC Analytics

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.text: The key numbers for whatever the filters select, at the top so you can see the size of the group before reading any rate.
steps.label: Headline figures

steps.title: How files progress, and grant rates
steps.text: Left, the files reaching each stage: leave decision, judicial review, judgment. Right, the share of leave decisions and of merits judgments granted, year by year.
steps.label: Progress

steps.title: How each year's files ended
steps.text: Leave refused, discontinued, dismissed, granted, settled, still open. Click a year and the whole page filters to it.
steps.label: Outcomes by year

steps.title: Who made the decision under review
steps.text: Leave grant rates by kind of decision challenged (RPD, RAD, PRRA, visa offices and so on), and the most frequent offices behind them. Click one to filter.
steps.label: Decision under review

steps.title: How long things take
steps.text: Median days between filing, leave decision and judicial review, with the middle half of files as a band; and days to the leave decision by year filed (years with under 30 decisions are left out).
steps.label: Time between steps

steps.title: Motions by type
steps.text: Ruled motions split granted and dismissed, plus withdrawn and never ruled. The grant rate counts ruled motions only.
steps.label: Motions

steps.title: Judges: leave versus judicial review
steps.text: Each dot is a judge with at least 25 leave decisions: leave grant rate across, judicial review grant rate up, dot size by decisions. Click a dot to filter to that judge.
steps.label: Judges

steps.title: Applicant counsel
steps.text: Counsel named on the applicant's side, with their files and rates. Click a row to see only their files.
steps.label: Counsel

steps.title: Deadlines and refusals
steps.text: Whether the application met the 15-day or 60-day limit in section 72 of IRPA and the Rule 10, 11 and 15 steps; and refusals where no record was filed against refusals on the record, which separates abandoned files from files that lost.
steps.label: Deadlines

steps.title: By registry
steps.text: Files by registry office with the leave grant rate. Click one to filter.
steps.label: Registries

steps.title: Try a filter
steps.text: I pressed Last 5 years. Every figure and chart now covers only files filed in those years, and the active filter shows so it can be removed.
steps.label: Last 5 years

steps.title: Read the rates with the caveats
steps.text: Rates use files with an observed decision, and counts sit beside every rate because small groups are not reliable. Motions never ruled on are inferred from what happened next, and Registry entries can contain errors.
steps.label: Caveats

steps.title: Your Workbench (demo)
steps.text: The tour signed you in as Demo analyst (no password; a made-up name keeps lists apart). The case list follows your IMM files: paste numbers or a column from Excel, and a flag shows when the stored Federal Court docket has moved.
steps.label: Demo analyst

steps.title: Your pinned decision
steps.text: Vavilov is here because the tour pinned it from the reader. Pins take folders and notes, and Compare selected sets two decisions side by side.
steps.label: Pinned decisions

steps.title: Document tools
steps.text: Two tools work on your own documents, in memory and never stored: Live analysis (next) reads a factum or memo against the library, and the De-identifier swaps names, ID numbers and dates for placeholders before a document goes anywhere else.
steps.label: Live analysis

steps.title: From a document to the right cases
steps.text: An analyst starts from a document, here a fictional Memorandum of Argument from a cessation judicial review, and ends with the cases that matter. I pasted it; a Word file or a text PDF works too. It is read in memory, never stored, and no AI is used.
steps.label: Your document

steps.title: The document, marked up
steps.text: I pressed Analyze. The bar counts the case citations and statute references found, and every one is marked in the text.
steps.label: Counts and layers

steps.title: Matched to the library
steps.text: This citation is matched to Vavilov in the library, with its pinpoint paragraphs. Short forms such as 'Vavilov, above at para 99' and 'Ibid' are traced back to the same case.
steps.label: In the library

steps.title: Statutes, and what we do not hold
steps.text: Provisions of IRPA and the Federal Courts Act are found and tied to the statute library. Cases the library does not hold are still marked, so you can see what cannot be checked here.
steps.label: Statute

steps.title: Every authority, and which ones we hold
steps.text: One table of every authority in the document: how it was written, whether it is in the library, and how often it is mentioned. This is the shortlist of cases to read for this argument. It also downloads as a spreadsheet.
steps.label: Authority table

steps.title: Pull those cases in one click
steps.text: Save library cases to Workbench takes every authority in the document that the library holds and pins it to your list, ready to open, compare and read. I pressed it for you.
steps.label: Saved
steps.writes: This step saved the library cases cited in the fictional MOA to the demo Workbench list. Remove them any time from the Workbench.

steps.title: The result: a reading list from the document
steps.text: The cases cited in the MOA that the library holds are now on your Workbench, with Vavilov among them. From here an analyst can open each one, add notes and compare decisions side by side.
steps.label: Pinned from the MOA

steps.title: That is the tour
steps.text: You have seen search and its filters, the formatted reader, judges, citation intelligence, Federal Court analytics, the Workbench and live document analysis. Take the tour again from the About page whenever you like. Press Done to explore on your own.
